title: Gnostic Awakenings: Science Fiction, Myth-Making, and the Religious Imagination
author: Daniel Atik
card_summary: A Wesleyan University honors thesis in Religion exploring the intersection of science fiction, myth-making, and the religious imagination. Examines how science fiction authors, including Philip K. Dick, engage with Gnostic themes and religious meaning-making through speculative storytelling.

## **Acknowledgements** 

In the early, inchoate stages of the development of this thesis, my advisor made a remark that writing a thesis is like constructing a monolith: you must build brick by brick, sentence by sentence, word by word. Like much of what they say, this proved prescient. Building this thesis was truly a labor that required a level of persistence and dogged determination that necessitated taking it step by step. 

There were numerous times during the course of completing this thesis where I was confronted with several debilitating setbacks, a good deal of crushing doubts, and anxieties about whether I would be able to finish at all. Surmounting these concerns would have been impossible without the support, assurances, and assistance offered by so many people. 

I would like to extend the utmost gratitude and appreciation for my advisor, Peter Gottschalk, for guiding me through all stages of completing this project even amidst a pandemic. Completing this thesis simply would not have been possible without his constant support and encouragement. 

My gratitude also extends to the entire Wesleyan religion department for influencing my growth throughout all four years of my experience here. I would especially like to thank Professor Rubenstein, Cameron, and Feller for their invaluable support in shaping my intellectual trajectory in the department through their steadfast guidance and brilliance. 

Numerous thanks to Professor Eudell and my entire Mellon Mays cohort for their incessant support through being a reliable resource throughout this semester. Spending these last past two years growing and learning with you guys has been an honor. 

I would also like to voice my appreciation to my dear friends, Nathan Cheng and Aryan Vavila, for being there for me for all four years of Wesleyan. You guys are an indelible part of my life. 

Lastly, I must thank my family, especially my parents and my sisters, Olivya and Jana, for constantly supporting me in all the endeavors I have undertaken, including this thesis.
